newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-BLACKS TAKE PRIDE IN WOODS'S MASTERS VICTORY.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-BLACKS TAKE PRIDE IN WOODS'S MASTERS VICTORY.

text.p: Tiger Woods's date with destiny on Sunday, when he became the first man of colour to win one of golf's four major championships, was the source of pride and optimism for many of the black people in the huge galleries at Augusta National Golf Club.
"He's just a great golfer. He's become the Michael Jordan of golf," Brandon Mason of Augusta said, referring to the professional basketball superstar.
"Remember when it was 'Be like Mike?' Now it's 'Be like Tiger,'" Mason added as he battled the crowds to get a glimpse of the 21-year-old Woods early in his round.
"He's inspiring. But it makes a difference that he is black -- there will be a lot more eyes on him."
Almost all eyes were on Woods when he drove off the first tee, including many of the exclusive club's black employees, who abandoned their duties briefly to watch Woods begin his historic round.

"He's awesome, just awesome," said Willie Brown, another local resident, who added that not only golf fans were aware of and interested in Woods precedent-setting performance, in which he set a Masters scoring record of 270 and won by the biggest margin ever, 12 shots.

"I called my mom last night and she doesn't know a par-3 from a par-4 but she was going on and on, 'What did you think about that Tiger Woods? He's something else. He gives me goosebumps just watching him.'"
Brown, like several other black fans who tried to follow Woods's progress on the crowded course, said the emergence of the young phenomenon would open golf's doors to all minorities.
"Tiger's going to put us in the mix," Brown said.

Keith Hodge, who drove to Augusta from Atlanta to witness the ascension of Woods to the pinnacle of a sport that not too long ago would not allow African-Americans to participate at the highest levels, agreed with Brown.
"They'll be a lot of new interest (in golf) because of him," Hodge said. "But it still costs a lot of money to play golf and a lot of blacks won't be able to afford it.
"All the blacks you see out here probably play anyway. Let's wait and see what Tiger means to golf in a year or two."
Still, the consensus among most fans watching Woods was that he would create a groundswell of interest in his sport among Americans in general, especially young people.
"I think he's good for golf as a whole," said Glenn Johnson, another Augusta resident. "A lot of people just knowing he'll be on TV will start watching golf for the first time."
"He's one in a million. He's going to increase the participation in golf for all races, I believe," said Arthur Mckenzie of Augusta. "It's a phenomenon."
"A whole generation of young people, not just blacks, are going to be influenced by this," said Tish Hodge, who was at the tournament with her brother-in-law.

Clara Johnson of Augusta said Woods's victory would inspire young people of colour to dream about the Masters, where blacks were not invited to play until Lee Elder gained entry in 1975 by virtue of a victory on the PGA tour.
Elder, Woods, Calvin Peete and Jim Thorpe are still the only black men to have played in the Masters.
"I think he'll encourage a lot of young people who never thought they could get to Augusta to say 'Hey, maybe I can,'" Johnson said.
